excerpt: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 32f -- Interventions: weight decay I'm still working on improving the test loss for a from-scratch GPT-2 small base model, trained on code based on Sebastian Raschka's book "Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)". In my training code, I have this code to create the optimiser: optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW( model.parameters(), lr=0.0004, weight_decay=0.1 ) In my last post I looked into the learning rate, the lr parameter in that code, and found a value for that, plus some extra code to schedule it -- that is, to vary it over time -- which gave better training results. This time I want to go into the weight decay. What is it, what is it for, and is 0.1 really the best value? I was a little concerned going into this that in order to understand this hyperparameter, I'd need to have a good understanding of how the optimiser works; I've been building what I think is a solid mental model of optimisers, but I don't think I understand them well enough to explain them yet, and I've been hoping to delay posting about them to a separate blog post series after this one. The good news is that while weight decay is an important aspect of how optimisers work -- the "W" in AdamW, the thing that makes it different to the older Adam optimiser, is a nod to its different treatment of weight decay -- you don't need to know how the optimiser itself works to understand what weight decay is. Instead, you just need to consider an older and more fundamental aspect of building ML systems -- regularisation. In order to dig into that, let's start with overfitting.
